title: Reconstruct Anything Model a lightweight general model for computational imaging
claim: One general model handles many inverse problems, in and out of distribution, turning degraded measurements into clean reconstructions without per-task training.
layout: 4 colored panels, two rows measurement over output, arrows between rows
description: A wide gallery figure with two rows of image pairs. The top row is labeled 'measurement' and shows degraded inputs. The bottom row is labeled 'RAM' and shows the clean reconstructions. Small gray arrows join each pair. The columns are grouped into four tinted panels. Yellow is in-distribution: motion blur, Gaussian tomography and singlecoil MRI. Green is out-of-distribution: Poisson tomography, multicoil MRI and satellite demosaicing. Pink is blind deblurring. Blue is self-supervised finetuning on OOD degradations and images: a SPAD camera and cryo-EM. The bold headers 'Zero-shot performance' and 'Self-supervised finetuning' sit above the panels, and italic captions below name each regime. The eye goes first to the contrast between noisy inputs and sharp RAM outputs. The panel colors then group the tasks by difficulty.
caption: The proposed Reconstruct Anything Model (RAM) model can solve a wide variety of inverse problems, from medical imaging to microscopy and low-photon imaging, obtaining state-of-the-art zero-shot performance in imaging problems and datasets in or close to the training distribution. RAM can also be finetuned in a self-supervised way (without any ground-truth references) for images and/or problems strongly differing from training distribution.
abstract: Most existing learning-based methods for solving imaging inverse problems can be roughly divided into two classes: iterative algorithms, such as plug-and-play and diffusion methods leveraging pretrained denoisers, and unrolled architectures that are trained end-to-end for specific imaging problems. Iterative methods in the first class are computationally costly and often yield suboptimal reconstruction performance, whereas unrolled architectures are generally problem-specific and require expensive training. In this work, we propose a novel non-iterative, lightweight architecture that incorporates knowledge about the forward operator (acquisition physics and noise parameters) without relying on unrolling. Our model is trained to solve a wide range of inverse problems, such as deblurring, magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, inpainting, and super-resolution, and handles arbitrary image sizes and channels, such as grayscale, complex, and color data. The proposed model can be easily adapted to unseen inverse problems or datasets with a few fine-tuning steps (up to a few images) in a self-supervised way, without ground-truth references. Throughout a series of experiments, we demonstrate state-of-the-art performance from medical imaging to low-photon imaging and microscopy. Our code is available at https://github.com/matthieutrs/ram.
